name: Bianca Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Bianca, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 1 at Oakfield Primary, a suburban primary school, so twenty-eight five- and six-year-olds. The day is phonics first thing, then maths with counting bears, then a lot of shoelaces, lost jumpers and someone crying because their tower fell over. I love the moment a child sounds out a word on their own for the first time; their whole face changes. What wears me out is the noise by half past two and the assessment spreadsheets on top of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside school? Who's at home, and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé Idris, who's an accountant at a mid-sized firm doing accounts for small businesses. We rent a terraced house and we're saving for a wedding next summer, so we've got about three months of bills put by plus the wedding pot. I'm fairly middle-of-the-road about most things. I use the AI chatbot now and then for the parents' newsletter, once a friend in Year 2 showed me it saved her an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's useful for small things and the rest was hype. Probably over dinner with the Year 2 teachers, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things carry on as they are, which is fine by me. Five-year-olds will always need a grown-up who can tie a shoelace and spot a fever. Pay is what it is, but it's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using it for the newsletter, and keep putting money in the wedding pot, about two hundred a month. Maybe I'd go for the phonics lead role next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at all that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual things: the school's budget, and whether we can afford a house before we're forty. Those were there before AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Idris? Does his work change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, he says. The software does more of the bank reconciliations, matching payments to invoices. But his clients still want a person to ring when the tax bill comes.

say: I'd say AI is **useful for small things** and the rest was hype.
I'd say it casually over **dinner** with colleagues, nothing dramatic.
think: I think five-year-olds will always need a **grown-up** who can tie shoelaces and spot fevers.
My pay is ordinary but **steady**, which suits me.
do: Keep using the chatbot for the **parents' newsletter**.
Put **£200 a month** into the wedding pot.
Apply for the **phonics lead** role next year.
S0.quote: Five-year-olds will always need a grown-up who can tie a shoelace and spot a fever.
fieldNote: Her early-years role is heavily **hands-on**, so the plateau barely touches it.
Her fiancé's **accounting job** is lightly affected but stable here.
Background worry about **buying a house** predates AI.

steps.text: Keep teaching phonics and maths to Year 1
Put £200 a month into the wedding pot
Apply for the school's phonics lead role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be bumpy for some jobs and we should help people through it. Sensible stuff, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the reports and assessment spreadsheets get easier, and that's it. Idris is the worry. Checking, booking and number-crunching is most of what a junior accountant like my fiancé Idris does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the school's new tools properly once they're proven, especially for reports. We'd move half the wedding pot into a general emergency fund. And Idris would start looking at advisory work, which needs a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, properly anxious for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Idris's firm uses software already. What happens there in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've already not replaced two people who left last year. If they cut again, he's not senior enough to be safe. He might keep his job but on less pay, or get moved to something he hates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that mean for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller, probably. We'd do the registry office and a pub lunch instead of the hotel. My mum would be upset, but she'd get over it.

say: I'd say it will be **bumpy** for some jobs and people need help through it.
think: I think my **reports** and spreadsheets get easier, and little else changes.
Idris is the worry, because **number-crunching** is most of a junior accountant's work.
do: Learn the school's **report tools** properly once they're proven.
Move half the **wedding pot** into an emergency fund.
Encourage Idris towards **advisory work** with clients in person.
S1.quote: Checking, booking and number-crunching is most of what a junior accountant like my fiancé Idris does.
fieldNote: Her own job is safe; the **household risk** is her fiancé's accounting role.
His firm already **left posts unfilled**, a concrete early sign.
She'd **scale down the wedding** without much drama, a pragmatic response.

steps.text: Learn the school's AI report-writing tool once proven
Move half the wedding pot into an emergency fund
Swap the hotel wedding for a registry office and pub lunch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to get a grip fast, because two years is nothing. I'd be practical about it: support for people losing jobs, and quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Idris loses his job in 2028 or soon after. Accountancy is pure thinking work. My job probably holds a few years longer, because robots aren't wiping noses until 2031 at the earliest, but then I'm the only earner on a teacher's salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd postpone the wedding and keep every penny. We'd cut the car and the gym. I'd pick up paid after-school tutoring for reading, a few evenings a week. And we'd talk to Idris's parents about moving in with them if it got bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. It's the sort of thing that sits on your chest at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is very hands-on with little ones. Does the three-year gap before robots matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot. A five-year-old needs someone to hold their hand crossing the road, and that doesn't come with a laptop. So I'd probably have work after 2028, and that buys us time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Idris that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we postpone the wedding, not cancel it, and that he's not going through it alone. Then I'd probably cry in the bath.

say: I'd say governments must **get a grip** fast, because two years is nothing.
I'd push for **quick support** for people losing jobs.
think: I think Idris **loses his job** in 2028 or soon after.
Then I'm the **only earner** on a teacher's salary until robots arrive.
do: **Postpone the wedding** and keep every penny saved.
Give up the **car and gym** straight away.
Tutor **reading after school** a few evenings a week.
feel: **Frightened**, the kind of fear that sits on your chest at 3am.
S2.quote: A five-year-old needs someone to hold their hand crossing the road, and that doesn't come with a laptop.
fieldNote: She sees her job as the **anchor** while her fiancé's goes early.
The **robot gap** matters a lot to her: years of hands-on work left.
Wedding becomes the first **postponed plan**; emotional but decisive.

steps.text: Postpone the wedding until both incomes are clearer
Give up the car and gym memberships

Ask Idris's parents about moving in if money runs short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan, and not just in governments. Families need to talk about this too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Idris has a few years to shift into something more people-facing, and I'm fine until 2034 or so. Then it's anyone's guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris would start an advisory or tax planning qualification next year. I'd keep teaching and go for the phonics lead role. We'd keep saving hard: aim for six months of bills by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a planning kind of anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years' warning, what would you do differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still the wedding, just smaller. You can't put your whole life on hold for five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether to have children. We'd talk about having one around 2030, while I'm still in a steady job and before anything big happens.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so we should actually plan.
Families need to talk about this, not just **governments**.
think: I think Idris has a few years to move into **people-facing** work.
I feel fine until **2034** or so, then it's anyone's guess.
do: Support Idris to start a **tax planning** qualification next year.
Keep teaching and go for the **phonics lead** role.
Save towards **six months** of bills by 2030.
feel: **Anxious**, but the kind of anxious that makes lists.
S3.quote: You can't put your whole life on hold for five years.
fieldNote: Her plans **centre on Idris** retraining into advisory accounting.
She'd still marry, **smaller**, and think about a child around 2030.
Her own **robot gap** to 2034 gives her a sense of breathing room.

steps.text: Help Idris enrol on a tax planning qualification

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of warning, and nobody should be caught out. Let's be grown-up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be fine. Idris has time to move into advisory work, I'd be well established, maybe a deputy head by then. The house is the bigger question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned next summer. Idris would retrain slowly. I'd learn whatever tools the school brings in once they're proven, and we'd start saving for a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, probably in three or four years. Renting forever on a teacher's salary feels riskier than buying a house before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe having kids. We'd have two by then, hopefully, so the timing of everything matters.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fair warning and nobody should be caught out.
think: I think we'd be **fine**, with Idris moving into advisory work in time.
The bigger question is **buying a house** before 2036.
do: Hold the **wedding** as planned next summer.
Start saving for a **house deposit** within three or four years.
Learn the school's **AI tools** once they're proven.
S4.quote: Renting forever on a teacher's salary feels riskier than buying a house before 2036.
fieldNote: The decade lets her keep **normal plans**: wedding, house, children.
Unease sits around **housing** and timing, not her classroom.
Trusts her fiancé can **retrain gradually** with this much warning.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Buy a house within three or four years
Learn new school AI tools once colleagues have proved them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Idris's job would go before we'd even married. What would help is real retraining money for people like him, and a promise that early years stays with people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what teachers think children should learn now. I'd say reading, kindness and resilience. Machines aren't going to teach a five-year-old to share the glue stick.

headlineQuote: Machines aren't going to teach a five-year-old to share the glue stick.
portrait: Bianca teaches **Year 1** at a suburban primary, a job full of shoelaces, phonics and noise.
She's engaged to **Idris**, an accountant whose number-crunching work is highly exposed.
Middle-of-the-road and **steady**, she uses AI for newsletters once friends showed her.
She's calm in the plateau but **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, expecting Idris's job to go first.
With time she'd keep normal plans, scaling the **wedding** and timing children around the risk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her fiancé's accounting job would go before they married.
whatWouldHelp: A promise that **early years** teaching stays with people.
